new_statements.second_reader_evidence: Opened, rendered pdf page 66 (printed p. 410, running head 'C.L. VOORHOEVE') to an image and read it directly. The deciding sentence is there word for word: 'The language has contrastive vowel nasalization and three tonemes: high, mid, and low.' The phoneme list preceding it also matches except that the reader's transcription flattens two superscripts (page shows p [p, p^f, mp, b, w] and k [k, k^x, ŋk, x, g]; the quote gives 'pf' and 'kx'); hence confirmed with minor differences. The passage opens 'The sound system of Uhunduni (Amuŋ dialect) contains the following consonant and vowel phonemes' and the preceding lines say the writer used 'an unpublished grammar and dictionary of the Amuŋ dia…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Damal (Amung dialect) is described as a tone language with three contrastive tonemes (high, mid, low) plus contrastive vowel nasalization; no statement about word stress or its position is made. A second, independent report (Bromley 1977: 475, from Ellenberger's CAMA literacy primers) says the language has 'four phonemic tones' marked in the orthography in certain contexts, so the tone count is unsettled (three vs four) but the tonal status is agreed.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Note the discrepancy between Voorhoeve's three tonemes (Van der Stap's Amung data) and Bromley/Ellenberger's four phonemic tones (northern Damal).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level phoneme inventory summary based on Van der Stap's unpublished grammar of the Amung (southern) dialect; no phrase/citation-form detail. Bromley 1977 p. 475 (file) adds, second-hand: 'One of the primers is devoted to teaching the marks used in certain contexts to distinguish four phonemic tones.'
new_statements.identity_note: Voorhoeve 1975 explicitly describes the Amung (Amuŋ) dialect, i.e. the southern Amungme/Amung-kal variety, using Van der Stap's unpublished data; Bromley 1977 / Ellenberger's four-tone statement concerns the northern Damal dialect (Ilaga-Beoga). Both fall under dama1272 (no separate glottocodes for the dialects; Onikal and Ninuhkal are further sub-varieties named in the 2014 UNIPA theses).
